To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the bounds on $m_W$ can be substantially weakened by the inclusion of higher dimensional operators in the effective Lagrangians.
the SM bounds are substantially modified in the presence of dimension-six operators, which appear in the effective Lagrangians of the SM.
the present experimental bounds of the Higgs mass can be significantly modified, by a factor of 2-3, in the presence of dimension 6 operators in the effective Lagrangians.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the interplay between the Higgs mass bounds, as obtained by radiative corrections to the $W$ mass, and effective theories, in the context of the Standard Model.
the interplay of the present experimental bounds, on the Higgs boson mass, with the effective Lagrangians approach to new physics.

the interplay between the bounds on the SM parameters, $m_H$ and $m_W$, with the effective parameters of the theory, $\alpha_i$, and the scale of new physics $\Lambda$. The results obtained here can be used to set bounds on the parameters of the SM effective theory, and to determine the range of the new physics scale.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the SM bounds are not as stringent as usually thought, and that they are strongly dependent on the presence of the new physics.
the present experimental bounds from $m_W$ and $m_H$ on the effective parameters $\alpha_i$ are not very strong.
the present SM bound on the Higgs boson mass is $m_H < 700$ GeV.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the present bounds on the Higg mass, obtained from the radiative corrections to the $W$ mass, are not as strong as they seem to be.
the bounds on $m_W$ and the Higgs mass can be used as a tool to constrain the scale of new physics and the effective parameters of the theory.
the bounds on $m_W$, $m_H$ and $\Lambda$ are not independent.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to obtain the SM bound of 114 GeV, one needs to assume a scale of new physics of at least 1.5 TeV.
the bounds on the SM Higgs mass from radiative corrections are not universal, but depend on the specific effective theory that is being used.
the SM bounds are not robust and can be substantially modified in the presence of new physics.
